name: Jeffersonian Classicism

revival_periods.note: The City Beautiful and the American campus recover the Jeffersonian temple-and-lawn diagram wholesale; McKim, Mead & White's restoration of the Rotunda after the 1895 fire is the hinge.
'Jeffersonian' red brick with white trim and a tetrastyle portico becomes the default American institutional dress, usually with the ideological argument removed.

lineage.note: The whole ideological point. Jefferson quotes the Maison Carree at Nimes for the Virginia Capitol and the Pantheon for the Rotunda, across seventeen centuries and an ocean, with no line of transmission whatever. A republic quoting a republic rather than a monarchy.

Palladio via the Leoni and Giacomo Leoni-derived English editions was Jefferson's 'bible', but he treated Palladio as a reliable transcriber of Roman antiquity rather than as a Venetian master to be imitated. The reference goes through Palladio to Rome, not to the Veneto.

The actual transmission: Virginia brickmasons, carpenters and joiners trained in the Tidewater Georgian trade built every Jeffersonian building. Monticello's Flemish bond, sash detail and interior joinery are Virginia Georgian craft executed to unfamiliar drawings.

Direct transmission, not quotation: Jefferson lived in Paris 1784-89, admired the Hotel de Salm to the point of remodelling Monticello around it, and collaborated with Charles-Louis Clerisseau, who drafted the Virginia Capitol model.
Explicitly and in writing. Jefferson called Williamsburg's buildings 'rude, mis-shapen piles' and set out to make the architecture of the new state unmistakably not English.
The Adamesque thinning that produced Federal is exactly what Jefferson refused: he wanted correct antique orders at correct antique weight, taken from measured plates, not fashionable attenuation.

description.short: Thomas Jefferson's Roman republicanism built in Virginia brick: correct antique orders taken directly from measured plates of Rome and from Palladio as their transcriber, deliberately bypassing the English intermediary that every other American builder was still working through.
description.long:
Jeffersonian Classicism is a small body of work by one amateur and his circle that changed what American public architecture was for. Formally it consists of a red brick body with white-painted wood or stuccoed trim, a portico of correct Roman orders scaled by module from published plates, a low pitched roof usually concealed behind a balustrade or a Chinese railing, and a plan built out of octagons, cubes and their halves. Its buildings look at first like well-made Georgian houses that have been rearranged by somebody with an unusual amount of geometry. Look longer and the Georgian conventions are all missing: no projecting frontispiece, no steep dormered roof, no fashionable Adam thinning of the orders, no visible service wing. Jefferson buried the dependencies in terraced L-shaped wings so that Monticello would read as a single-storey villa, which is both a compositional trick and an act of concealment about who did the work.

The conditions are unusually explicit, because the man wrote them down. The Revolution had produced a state that needed buildings and had no architectural language it could use without embarrassment: Georgian was the architecture of the Crown, and there was nothing else. Jefferson, in Paris as minister from 1784, solved the problem by going around England altogether. For the Virginia Capitol he chose the Maison Carree at Nimes, a first-century Roman temple, and had Charles-Louis Clerisseau draft the model; he substituted a Scamozzian Ionic for the original Corinthian because Virginia workmen could cut it. That decision - a modern legislature housed in a Roman temple, the first anywhere in the world - established the temple form as the American public building type and did so on an argument, not a fashion. The mechanism of transmission was books and one man's obsession: Palladio's Quattro Libri in English editions, Fréart de Chambray, Gibbs, Robert Morris, and later the measured antiquities of Desgodetz. The mechanism of execution was ordinary Virginia craft. Monticello was built and rebuilt for forty years by a rotating labour force that included enslaved brickmakers, carpenters and joiners - John Hemmings among them - working Georgian trade methods to non-Georgian drawings. Any honest account of this style has to hold both facts at once: it is the architecture of stated liberty, and it was built by people who did not have any.

What it reacts against is England, specifically and consciously. Jefferson's private verdict on Williamsburg - 'rude, mis-shapen piles' - is the founding statement of the style, and his choice of Rome over London is not aesthetic preference but constitutional argument: a republic should quote a republic. This is what separates the node from federal-style, which was busy importing Robert Adam's London fashion at the same moment and building beautifully with it. Federal is up-to-date; Jeffersonian is deliberately ancient. Federal thins the orders for elegance; Jefferson insisted on correct entasis and correct entablature depth because correctness was the point. It is also why the style barely propagates as domestic architecture: an argument does not scale into a builder's trade the way a plate of mouldings does. Its real inheritance runs through public buildings and campuses for the next century and a half.

Standing at Monticello's west front you understand the geometry before you understand the ornament. The dome sits on a low octagon and the whole house presents as one storey, which at the actual size of the building is a lie the eye accepts gratefully; the mezzanine windows are tucked under the entablature so that the second floor is invisible from outside. Inside, the rooms are octagons and half-octagons, and the light comes through triple-sash windows and skylights that make the plan feel larger and stranger than its footprint. At Poplar Forest the argument is purer still: an octagonal house around a twenty-foot cube of a dining room lit only from a skylight, so that at midday there is a column of light standing in the middle of the house. At the University of Virginia the diagram becomes urbanism - ten pavilions, each demonstrating a different correct order as a teaching specimen, joined by a colonnade and terminated by a half-scale Pantheon holding a library instead of an altar. It is the most complete piece of architectural reasoning produced in America, and it is made of the same brick as every tobacco warehouse in the county.

defining_characteristics: Orders taken from measured plates of Roman antiquity (or from Palladio as their transcriber) at correct antique proportion, never attenuated for fashion
Red brick laid in Flemish bond with white-painted wood or stuccoed trim; material palette essentially fixed
Temple-derived portico used as the governing gesture on public buildings and as a full-height entrance feature on houses
Plan geometry built from octagons, cubes, and their halves rather than from the rectangular Georgian room grid
Low roof pitch concealed behind balustrade, railing or parapet so the building reads as a single classical volume
Service and secondary storeys suppressed - dependencies terraced or sunk, mezzanines hidden behind the entablature - so the mass reads simpler than it is
Ideological intent: the classical form is chosen as a political argument about the form of government, and the choice bypasses English precedent on purpose
diagnostic_tells: A house that appears to be one storey but is demonstrably two, with small square mezzanine windows tucked directly under the cornice
Octagonal or semi-octagonal room projections in plan, visible as canted bays on the elevation
Portico entablature of correct Roman depth (roughly a fifth of column height) where a Federal house of the same date would have a thin cornice and no portico at all
Chinese-lattice roof railing or a balustrade concealing a nearly flat roof
Dependencies running out sideways at or below grade rather than as visible flanking wings above ground

distinguished_from.difference: Contemporaneous and opposite in method. Federal takes Adam's London fashion and thins the orders; Jefferson takes Rome directly and keeps them at antique weight. Federal's signature is the elliptical fanlight in a flat wall; Jefferson's is a correct portico and an octagon in plan. If the classicism looks archaeologically argued rather than fashionably light, it is Jeffersonian.

Both use full porticoes, but Jeffersonian orders are Roman (Tuscan, Doric with a base, Ionic, Corinthian, arches and domes permitted) while Greek Revival orders are Greek (baseless Doric, no arches, no domes). A dome or a round-headed arch rules out Greek Revival immediately.

The twentieth-century revival copies the temple front and the red brick but at institutional scale, with steel behind the brick, plate glass, and no interest in the geometry of the plan. Jeffersonian buildings are small, hand-built, and the octagons are real.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Classical orders with the module set as the lower column diameter, taken from published measured plates rather than from local practice; overall dimensioning by simple whole-number ratios and by the octagon, which Jefferson used as a room-generating figure rather than as a curiosity.
typical_ratios: Roman Doric 8 diameters, Ionic 9, Corinthian 10, with entablature 1/4 to 1/5 of column height
Cubic and near-cubic rooms: Poplar Forest's dining room is 20 x 20 x 20 feet
Octagonal rooms generated on a square, canted corners at 1/3 of the side
Roof pitch 3:12 or lower, concealed; parapet or railing at least 3 feet high
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even bay rhythm derived from the portico's intercolumniation and carried across the whole elevation; the portico sets the module and the walls obey it, rather than the portico being fitted to a pre-existing wall.

massing_affinities.note: But with the flanking dependencies terraced into the slope rather than raised as visible pavilions - Jefferson's characteristic inversion of the Palladian scheme.
Poplar Forest is the first octagonal house in America; the figure recurs as room shape throughout the style.
The underlying Virginia Georgian plan, geometrically disturbed.
Bremo and the pavilions at the University; the wings are colonnades rather than domestic ells.

constraints.statement: Orders must be executed at correct antique proportion: Roman Doric at 8 lower diameters, Ionic at 9, Corinthian at 10, with entablature depth 1/4 to 1/5 of column height. Attenuated columns above 10 diameters convert the building to Federal.

test.note: 1/4 to 1/5 of column height, order-independent. The order-specific diameter figures (Doric 8, Ionic 9, Corinthian 10) and the above-10-diameters-reads-as-Federal ceiling stay prose.

constraints.statement: Round-headed arches, domes and semicircular (Diocletian) windows are permitted and characteristic; the Greek baseless Doric column and the frieze-band attic window are forbidden. Roman and Greek vocabularies must not be mixed on one building.
Roof pitch must not exceed 4:12 and must be concealed behind a balustrade, Chinese railing or parapet at least 3 feet high. Dormers on a principal elevation are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the 4:12 roof-pitch ceiling. The concealment requirement (balustrade/railing/parapet at least 3ft high, testable via parapet_height_in) and the no-dormers-on-a-principal-elevation clause (testable via front_slope_dormer_count = 0) are also cleanly expressible but left as prose here since the schema allows one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Service dependencies must be terraced, sunk below the principal floor level, or run out as low L-wings whose roofs form usable terraces, so that the main block reads as a single volume. A visible two-storey service wing breaks the parti.

Material palette is fixed: red brick in Flemish bond with white-painted trim and, where used, stuccoed or sanded-paint columns imitating stone. Painted brick, stone facing, or contrasting trim colours fall outside the style.

exemplars.name: Virginia State Capitol
exemplars.note: Cornerstone 1785; occupied by the General Assembly 1788, finished later. Modelled on the Maison Carree at Nimes with Jefferson substituting Scamozzian Ionic for Corinthian. The first modern legislative building anywhere to take the form of a classical temple.

exemplars.name: Monticello
exemplars.note: Begun 1768, rebuilt from 1794 after Jefferson's return from France, substantially complete 1809. Octagonal dome, suppressed second storey, terraced L-shaped dependencies.

exemplars.name: Poplar Forest
exemplars.note: Begun 1806. Octagonal plan around a 20-foot cubic dining room lit by a skylight; probably the first octagonal house built in the United States.

exemplars.name: The Rotunda and Academical Village, University of Virginia
exemplars.note: Begun 1817. Ten pavilions each demonstrating a different correct order, joined by colonnades and terminated by a half-scale Pantheon housing the library rather than an altar.

sources: William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: The Colonial and Neoclassical Styles (1970)
Andrea Palladio, I Quattro Libri dell'Architettura (1570), in the English editions Jefferson owned
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
Richard Guy Wilson, Thomas Jefferson's Academical Village (2009)

proportion_packs.note: PALLADIO OVER GIBBS OR BENJAMIN, AND THIS IS THE LOAD-BEARING CHOICE FOR THE WHOLE NODE. The style's own lineage explicitly makes Palladio -- via the English editions Jefferson called his 'bible' -- his source, and just as explicitly separates that from the Tidewater Georgian craft channel his masons and joiners actually came out of ('descends_from tidewater-georgian... Virginia brickmasons... trained in the Tidewater Georgian trade built every Jeffersonian building'). Both gibbs-ionic and benjamin-ionic are architecturally present in this corpus and gibbs-ionic is even listed in this node's own applies_to cross-reference, but binding either here would blur exactly the distinction the style file draws against english-georgian ('rude, mis-shapen piles') -- Jefferson's DESIGN authority is Palladio-as-transcriber-of-Rome, not the pattern-book tradition his craftsmen executed to. The fit is also numerically exact: this pack's column is 9 Palladian modules, i.e. 9 diameters, matching the style's own stated 'Ionic 9' precisely -- and it is the order of the Virginia Capitol, where Jefferson substituted a Scamozzian Ionic for the Maison Carree's original Corinthian because Virginia workmen could cut it.

The style's own stated 'Roman Doric 8 diameters' matches this pack's column exactly (16 semidiameter-modules = 8 diameters, identical to vignola-doric's figure since Palladio's Doric differs from Vignola's only in entasis and fluting, not in overall height). Demonstrated at the University of Virginia's Academical Village, where Doric is one of the ten orders the pavilions use as teaching specimens.

A THIRD ORDER IS BOUND HERE, UNLIKE ANY OTHER NODE IN THIS BATCH, because Jefferson's own practice genuinely deployed three correct Roman orders side by side as a stated pedagogical program at the University of Virginia, and because Corinthian was the Capitol's ORIGINAL order before Jefferson's Ionic substitution. Flagged honestly: the style states 'Corinthian 10' diameters but this pack's Palladian Corinthian column is 9.5 -- a half-diameter short of an exact match, the closest the corpus's 36 packs get, and left as a visible discrepancy rather than rounded away.

JUDGMENT CALL, STATED AS SUCH. None of the pack's three named families (wall_section_georgian / _federal / _greek_revival) is a clean fit for interiors built to correct antique weight rather than to any of those three American traditions. wall_section_georgian is bound as the closer analogue -- full relief, carved, NOT the flattened Federal composition-ornament family Jefferson explicitly rejected ('Federal thins the orders for elegance; Jefferson insisted on correct entasis and correct entablature depth because correctness was the point') -- but this is an approximation the pack was not built for, not a documented fit.

Governs door and window sizing generally, beneath constraint c02's hard co-occurrence rule: round-headed arches, domes and semicircular Diocletian windows are permitted and characteristic, while the Greek baseless Doric and frieze-band attic window are forbidden outright -- Roman and Greek vocabularies must never mix on one building. No pack among the 36 encodes Diocletian/lunette window geometry specifically; that stays prose in the style file, a genuine gap.

The glazing module, bound but genuinely minor here -- the style file names no sash pattern or muntin width at all among its diagnostic tells, unlike federal-style or new-england-federal, because triple-sash windows and skylights (Monticello, Poplar Forest) carry more of Jefferson's fenestration argument than muntin count does.

Governs the temple-front portico and the bay rhythm its intercolumniation sets for the wall behind (2.25-2.5 diameters, Palladian eustyle, per the style's own proportional_system) -- and this is arguably the single most apt use of this pack in the whole batch, since georgian-colonial-american's own binding of it cites 'Palladio Book I chs. XXI-XXVI' as its authority, and here that authority is not once-removed through Gibbs but the building's actual named source.

Governs the literal floor-to-floor ratios but does not model Jefferson's real trick -- the suppressed second storey, mezzanine windows tucked directly under the entablature so a demonstrably two-storey house 'reads as one storey' from outside (the style's own leading diagnostic tell). That is visual concealment, not proportional diminution, and no pack among the 36 addresses it; a genuine gap distinct from the ordinary storey-height coverage this pack does provide.

Bound for the cubic and near-cubic rooms the style states directly -- Poplar Forest's dining room is 20 x 20 x 20 ft -- which is exactly this pack's harmonic-ratio domain. It does NOT model the octagon-on-a-square construction that is Jefferson's own specific and most distinctive room-generating figure (Poplar Forest's plan, the Rotunda's flanking rooms); no pack among the 36 encodes octagonal room geometry by name, so the general harmonic-ratio machinery is the closest available fit and the octagon itself stays prose. A genuine, acknowledged gap.

The material palette is fixed rather than optional at the level of the building (constraint c05: red brick in Flemish bond with white-painted or stuccoed trim; painted brick, stone facing or contrasting trim colours fall outside the style), but the pack itself is bound at the same optional role the rest of this batch uses for masonry modules, consistent with the corpus's own applies_to cross-reference for this node.

THE OTHER OCTAGON ENTIRELY, and the node that states its rule: 'octagonal rooms generated on a square, canted corners at 1/3 of the side', with 'plan geometry built from octagons, cubes, and their halves rather than from the rectangular Georgian room grid'. This is a ROOM and not a building -- take a square, cut each corner back a third, and the result sits comfortably inside a rectangular plan. That record also gives the elevation consequence the pack's bay rule is about: 'octagonal or semi-octagonal room projections in plan, visible as canted bays on the elevation'. Take the canted-corner rule and the bay rule here; leave every rule that begins from a regular octagon's side, because this house has none.
